checks.prompt: A team is choosing an approach for a voice-controlled kiosk that has no network connection and must show words as the user speaks. Another team is starting a greenfield product needing accurate, punctuated transcripts of multilingual interviews. Which team does this engine suit, and what is the crucial caveat they must plan around?
checks.explanation: The engine's genuine strengths are being fully offline and private, small enough for edge hardware, and streaming — the recurrent layer is deliberately unidirectional so partial results can be emitted while audio is still arriving. The blocking caveat is maintenance: development stopped, the runtime targets an old Python range, and the released model is English. A greenfield multilingual project wanting punctuation and robustness to noise is exactly what modern turnkey models do better.
options: The kiosk team: it is fully offline, small enough for modest hardware, and its recurrent layer runs in one direction so it can emit partial results as audio arrives. The caveat is that the project is archived — no new models or fixes, and its runtime targets an old range of Python versions — so the practical choice is its maintained successor or a deliberate decision to freeze the stack. The interview team should not use it: it is English-centric out of the box and weaker on noisy or accented speech than modern models
The interview team: its language model scorer supplies punctuation and multilingual coverage, while a kiosk needs a streaming model, which this architecture cannot provide
Both: the same model handles offline streaming and multilingual punctuated transcription, and being archived affects only new feature development
Neither: it produces character probabilities but has no decoder, so both teams need a separate recognition system on top

checks.prompt: Explain this engine with the 'reading sound left to right, one character at a time' picture. Walk the pipeline from waveform to text, naming each stage. Then explain the two mantras — that the alignment is learned for you, and that the acoustic model proposes while a language model disposes — and say what each one means for how you train and how you deploy.
checks.expected: A correct answer must walk the pipeline: sixteen-kilohertz mono samples are framed and reduced to a small vector of cepstral coefficients per frame — a twenty-five millisecond window every ten milliseconds, so about a hundred frames a second; each frame is concatenated with several frames of past and future context before the first layer; a few dense layers feed a recurrent layer, then a final dense layer and a distribution over the alphabet plus a blank symbol for every frame; and a decoding step turns that per-frame sequence into a string. The first mantra must be explained as replacing the classic pipeline: you supply audio and the transcript STRING, never the timing, and the training loss sums over every way the string could align to the frames, so no pronunciation dictionary, no forced alignment and no hidden-state model is needed. The role of the blank must be given: it lets the network say 'nothing new here' and is what allows a genuine double letter to survive the collapsing of repeats. The second mantra must be explained as a deployment fact: the network emits raw character probabilities that need not spell real words, and an external n-gram language model re-ranks candidate transcriptions during a beam search so the output reads like language — it is a separate file from the acoustic model, so it can be swapped or rebuilt for a specific domain without retraining the network, which is a cheap and high-leverage customisation. A strong answer notes that omitting it costs a lot of accuracy, and that streaming works by feeding chunks into a stream object and asking for intermediate decodes rather than calling the one-shot method repeatedly, which would lose context across chunks.

checks.prompt: A developer reports that transcription quality is poor. Investigating, you find they read a 44.1 kHz stereo file, converted the samples to floats in the range minus one to one, and passed them to the one-shot transcription call without enabling any external scorer. Rank the problems and say what each costs.
checks.explanation: The input contract is genuinely strict: sixteen kilohertz, mono, sixteen-bit integer samples. Nothing resamples or downmixes for you, and handing floating-point samples to an interface expecting integers produces garbage rather than an error. Separately, the external n-gram language model is what makes output read like real words — decoding without it is purely acoustic and the word error rate jumps noticeably. All three are worth fixing, and none of them is automatic.
options: Three separate problems. The audio contract is strict — sixteen kilohertz, single channel, sixteen-bit integer samples — and violating any part of it degrades accuracy silently or errors rather than being corrected for you; converting to floats in particular produces nonsense because the interface expects integer samples. And skipping the external language model leaves decoding purely acoustic, which costs a large amount of accuracy on its own
Only the sample rate matters; the channel count is averaged automatically and float samples are accepted, while the external scorer changes speed rather than accuracy
The float conversion is correct and expected; the real problems are the sample rate and the missing scorer, and the scorer would also handle the resampling
All three are cosmetic: the model normalises rate, channels and sample format internally, so the poor quality must come from the beam width default

checks.prompt: Implement the front-end arithmetic and the accuracy metric. Define `SR = 16000`, `WIN_MS = 25`, `HOP_MS = 10`, `N_MFCC = 26` and `N_CONTEXT = 9`. Write `window_samples(sample_rate=SR)` and `hop_samples(sample_rate=SR)` converting those millisecond figures to sample counts, and `n_frames(num_samples, sample_rate=SR)` returning 0 when the clip is shorter than one window and otherwise `1 + (num_samples - window) // hop`. Write `input_width()` returning the number of features the first layer receives per step, given each frame is concatenated with `N_CONTEXT` frames of past AND future context. Write `check_audio(sample_rate, channels, dtype)` returning True only for 16000 hertz, one channel and `"int16"`, raising `ValueError` naming the offending property otherwise. Write `wer_counts(reference, hypothesis)` splitting both on whitespace and returning `{"substitutions", "insertions", "deletions", "reference_words"}` from a minimum-edit-distance alignment of the two word sequences — where an insertion is a word present in the hypothesis but not the reference and a deletion is the reverse — raising `ValueError` for an empty reference. Write `wer(reference, hypothesis)` returning the three counts summed and divided by the number of reference words. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: The framing arithmetic is worth internalising because every shape downstream follows from it: a window every ten milliseconds means about a hundred frames a second whatever the clip length, and a clip shorter than one analysis window produces no frames at all. The input width assertion catches a common misreading — the first layer does not receive one frame's coefficients, it receives nineteen frames' worth, because each step is stacked with context either side. The metric block is where the interesting properties live. Notice that the score is not a percentage of correctness: a transcript that invents words can exceed one, because the denominator is the number of REFERENCE words rather than the length of what was produced. That also makes it asymmetric — swapping the two strings gives a different number — which is exactly why it must always be computed against a ground-truth reference and never in the other direction.
checks.test:
# The front end frames the waveform: a 25 ms window every 10 ms, so about a hundred
# frames a second regardless of how long the clip is.
assert window_samples() == 400 and hop_samples() == 160
assert n_frames(16_000) == 98
assert n_frames(5 * 16_000) == 498
assert n_frames(10 * 16_000) == 998
for seconds in (1, 5, 10, 30):
    assert abs(n_frames(seconds * 16_000) / seconds - 100) < 3, seconds
# A clip shorter than one analysis window yields nothing at all.
assert n_frames(399) == 0
assert n_frames(400) == 1
assert n_frames(559) == 1 and n_frames(560) == 2
assert n_frames(0) == 0

# Each step feeds the first layer the frame PLUS nine frames either side, which is
# where the input width comes from -- it is not the number of coefficients.
assert input_width() == 494
assert input_width() == (2 * 9 + 1) * 26
assert input_width() != N_MFCC

# The audio contract is strict, and the failure mode without it is silent damage
# rather than an error -- so it is worth checking explicitly.
assert check_audio(16_000, 1, "int16") is True
for bad in ((44_100, 1, "int16"), (8_000, 1, "int16"), (16_000, 2, "int16"),
            (16_000, 1, "float32"), (16_000, 1, "int32")):
    try:
        check_audio(*bad)
    except ValueError:
        continue
    raise AssertionError(f"{bad} must be refused")

# Word error rate counts the three kinds of mistake against the reference length.
perfect = wer_counts("the cat sat on the mat", "the cat sat on the mat")
assert perfect == {"substitutions": 0, "insertions": 0, "deletions": 0,
                   "reference_words": 6}, perfect
assert wer("the cat sat on the mat", "the cat sat on the mat") == 0.0

substituted = wer_counts("the cat sat on the mat", "the cat sat on a mat")
assert substituted["substitutions"] == 1, substituted
assert substituted["insertions"] == 0 and substituted["deletions"] == 0
assert abs(wer("the cat sat on the mat", "the cat sat on a mat") - 1 / 6) < 1e-12

deleted = wer_counts("the cat sat on the mat", "the cat sat the mat")
assert deleted == {"substitutions": 0, "insertions": 0, "deletions": 1,
                   "reference_words": 6}, deleted

inserted = wer_counts("the cat sat on the mat", "the big cat sat on the mat")
assert inserted == {"substitutions": 0, "insertions": 1, "deletions": 0,
                    "reference_words": 6}, inserted

mixed = wer_counts("the quick brown fox", "the quick red fox jumped")
assert mixed["substitutions"] == 1 and mixed["insertions"] == 1, mixed
assert mixed["deletions"] == 0, mixed
assert abs(wer("the quick brown fox", "the quick red fox jumped") - 0.5) < 1e-12

# The metric is not a percentage of correctness: a transcript that invents words can
# score above one.
assert wer("hello", "hello there my old friend") == 4.0
assert wer("one two three", "") == 1.0
assert wer("one two three", "four five six") == 1.0

# It is asymmetric, because the denominator is the REFERENCE length.
assert wer("a b", "a b c d") != wer("a b c d", "a b")
assert wer("a b", "a b c d") == 1.0
assert wer("a b c d", "a b") == 0.5

# Whitespace is not a word, and an empty reference has no denominator to divide by.
assert wer("  the   cat  ", "the cat") == 0.0
try:
    wer("", "anything")
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("an empty reference must be refused")

# The three counts always sum to the edit distance between the two word sequences.
for reference, hypothesis in [("a b c", "a x c"), ("a b c", "a c"),
                              ("a b c", "a b b c"), ("x y z", "a b c"),
                              ("one", "one one one")]:
    counts = wer_counts(reference, hypothesis)
    total = counts["substitutions"] + counts["insertions"] + counts["deletions"]
    assert abs(wer(reference, hypothesis) * len(reference.split()) - total) < 1e-12

checks.prompt: A team maintaining a legacy deployment wants to improve accuracy on their domain's jargon without retraining anything expensive, and to move the same system onto a handheld device. What are the two right moves?
checks.explanation: The separation of the acoustic network from the language model is the practical lever here: the scorer is its own file built from text, so generating one from in-domain material and attaching it biases decoding toward your vocabulary with no retraining of the network at all. And the acoustic model ships in two builds — a memory-mapped one that is faster on desktop and server, and a smaller quantised one meant for mobile and embedded — so matching the build to the platform is the move for the handheld. Repeatedly calling the one-shot method on chunks is the wrong pattern for live audio, because it discards context between chunks.
options: Build a domain-specific external language model and attach it at load time: the acoustic network and the language model are separate files, so a new scorer can be generated from in-domain text and swapped in without touching the network — a cheap, high-leverage change. For the handheld, switch from the memory-mapped desktop build of the acoustic model to the smaller quantised build intended for mobile and embedded targets
Fine-tune the acoustic model on jargon recordings, since the language model cannot affect vocabulary; and for the handheld, reduce the sample rate to halve the compute
Increase the beam width, which is what incorporates domain vocabulary; and for the handheld, run the same desktop build but disable the external scorer to save memory
Retrain both models together, since they share a vocabulary file; and for the handheld, split the audio into shorter chunks and call the one-shot method repeatedly

checks.prompt: Compare this engine with its maintained successor, with a turnkey multilingual transcription model, with a self-supervised model you fine-tune, and with a hosted cloud service. Say what each is best at. Then advise a hospital building an offline dictation tool for clinicians: no audio may leave the building, partial text should appear as the clinician speaks, and the vocabulary is heavily specialised. Say what you would build on and why, and name the one risk you would flag.
checks.expected: A correct answer must position all four. This engine is best for fully offline, streaming, small-footprint recognition and for understanding or maintaining alignment-free end-to-end systems; its weaknesses are that it is archived, English-centric out of the box, tied to an old runtime, and weaker on noise and accents than modern models. Its maintained successor keeps the same design, format and interface with ongoing upkeep and more languages, at the cost of a smaller community. The turnkey transcription model gives the best transcript for the least effort — multilingual, punctuated, cased, robust to noise — but is heavier, is not truly streaming, and can invent text over silence. The self-supervised model is the right base when you have in-domain audio and few labels and want open weights to fine-tune, though its plain output lacks casing and punctuation and needs a language model for the best accuracy. A hosted cloud service gives the highest accuracy with no operations, at the cost of money, a network dependency and audio leaving the premises — which the hospital's constraint rules out outright. The recommendation must satisfy all three constraints: offline and streaming point at this family, so the maintained successor rather than the archived original is the honest choice; and the specialised vocabulary is addressed by generating a domain-specific external language model from clinical text and attaching it, which needs no retraining of the acoustic network. Fine-tuning a self-supervised model on in-domain audio is a defensible alternative if the answer acknowledges it is not natively streaming. The risk to flag must be about longevity or accuracy in context — an archived or thinly maintained stack underneath a clinical tool, and the fact that this family is weaker on accented or noisy speech, which in a clinical setting is a safety-relevant accuracy question requiring measurement on real recordings rather than a published benchmark.
